claim: IFNγ is a key cytokine in protective immunity that induces major histocompatibility complex class II molecules (MHCII) to amplify CD4+ T cell activation and effector function.
source: Interferon-gamma (IFNγ) is a key cytokine in protective immunity that induces major histocompatibility complex class II molecules (MHCII) to amplify CD4+ T cell activation and effector function.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about IFNγ function and is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise.

claim: A genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen in murine macrophages identified genes that control MHCII surface expression.
source: Using a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen in murine macrophages, we identified genes that control MHCII surface expression.
evidence: The screen was performed and results are presented in the manuscript, including Figure 1 and associated data.

claim: GSK3β and MED16 are required for IFNγ-mediated induction of the MHCII transactivator Ciita.
source: Both pathways control distinct aspects of the IFNγ response and are necessary for IFNγ-mediated induction of the MHCII transactivator Ciita, MHCII expression, and CD4+ T cell activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced Ciita expression in knockout cells (Figures 2E, 3C).

claim: GSK3β and MED16 control IFNγ-mediated MHCII expression through two parallel pathways.
source: Mechanistic studies uncovered two parallel pathways of IFNγ-mediated MHCII control that require the multifunctional glycogen synthase kinase three beta (GSK3β) or the mediator complex subunit 16 (MED16).
evidence: This is supported by data showing independent effects of GSK3β and MED16 loss (Figure 4A) and distinct transcriptional profiles (Figure 5).

claim: Loss of either MED16 or GSK3β prevents effective activation of CD4+ T cells.
source: Both pathways control distinct aspects of the IFNγ response and are necessary for IFNγ-mediated induction of the MHCII transactivator Ciita, MHCII expression, and CD4+ T cell activation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by T cell activation assays showing reduced IFNγ production by NR1 cells when co-cultured with knockout macrophages (Figure 6).

claim: The binding of the T cell receptor (TCR) to the peptide-loaded MHCII on the surface of APCs is necessary for both CD4+ T cell activation and their continued effector function in peripheral tissues.
source: For CD4+ T cells, the binding of the T cell receptor (TCR) to the peptide-loaded major histocompatibility complex class II (MHCII) on the surface of APCs is necessary for both CD4+ T cell activation and their continued effector function in peripheral tissues (Tubo and Jenkins, 2014; DeSandro et al., 1999; Reith et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dysregulation of MHCII control leads to a variety of conditions including the development of autoimmunity and increased susceptibility to pathogens and cancers.
source: Dysregulation of MHCII control leads to a variety of conditions including the development of autoimmunity and increased susceptibility to pathogens and cancers (Koyama et al., 2011; Abrahimi et al., 2016; Thelemann et al., 2016; Johnson et al., 2016; Steimle et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: MHCII is constitutively expressed on dendritic cells and B cells.
source: While MHCII is constitutively expressed on dendritic cells and B cells, the production of the cytokine IFNγ promotes MHCII expression broadly in other cellular populations including macrophages (Jakubzick et al., 2017; Unanue et al., 2016; Collins et al., 1984; Neefjes et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: IFNγ production promotes MHCII expression broadly in cellular populations including macrophages.
source: While MHCII is constitutively expressed on dendritic cells and B cells, the production of the cytokine IFNγ promotes MHCII expression broadly in other cellular populations including macrophages (Jakubzick et al., 2017; Unanue et al., 2016; Collins et al., 1984; Neefjes et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: IFNγ-producing CD4+ T cells induce myeloid MHCII expression, which in turn amplifies CD4+ T cell responses in a feedforward loop.
source: The induction of MHCII in these tissues activates a feedforward loop wherein IFNγ-producing CD4+ T cells induce myeloid MHCII expression, which in turn amplifies CD4+ T cell responses (Neefjes et al., 2011; Buxadé et al., 2018; Ivashkiv, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Binding of IFNγ to its receptor induces cytoskeletal and membrane rearrangement that results in the activation of JAK1 and JAK2 and STAT1-dependent transcription.
source: Binding of IFNγ to its receptor induces cytoskeletal and membrane rearrangement that results in the activation of JAK1 and JAK2 and STAT1-dependent transcription (Bousoik and Montazeri Aliabadi, 2018; Hu and Ivashkiv, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: STAT1 induces Irf1, which then drives the expression of the MHCII master regulator, Ciita.
source: STAT1 induces Irf1, which then drives the expression of the MHCII master regulator, Ciita (Schroder et al., 2004; Lehtonen et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The activation of CIITA opens the chromatin environment surrounding the MHCII locus and recruits transcription factors, including CREB1 and RFX5.
source: The activation of CIITA opens the chromatin environment surrounding the MHCII locus and recruits transcription factors, including CREB1 and RFX5 (Reith et al., 2005; Beresford and Boss, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MHCII is regulated post-translationally to control the trafficking, peptide loading, and stability of MHCII on the surface of cells.
source: MHCII is also regulated post-translationally to control the trafficking, peptide loading, and stability of MHCII on the surface of cells (Paul et al., 2011; Oh et al., 2013; Alix et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In non-inflammatory conditions, macrophages express low levels of MHCII that is uniquely dependent on NFAT5.
source: In non-inflammatory conditions, macrophages express low levels of MHCII that is uniquely dependent on NFAT5 (Buxadé et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Basal MHCII expression on macrophages is insufficient to control intracellular bacterial pathogens, which require IFNγ-activation to propagate protective CD4+ T cell responses.
source: While basal MHCII expression on macrophages plays a role in graft rejection, it is insufficient to control intracellular bacterial pathogens, which require IFNγ-activation to propagate protective CD4+ T cell responses (Ankley et al., 2020; Grau et al., 1998; Underhill et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Many pathogens including Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Chlamydia trachomatis inhibit IFNγ-mediated MHCII induction to evade CD4+ T-cell-mediated control and drive pathogen persistence.
source: Many pathogens including Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Chlamydia trachomatis inhibit IFNγ-mediated MHCII induction to evade CD4+ T-cell-mediated control and drive pathogen persistence (Pai et al., 2003; Pennini et al., 2006; Zhong et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Clone L3 Cas9+ iBMDMs showed 85-99% editing efficiency when targeting CD11b with sgRNAs.
source: Using the same Cd11b sgRNAs in a clonal population (clone L3) we found 85–99% of cells were deficient in CD11b expression by flow cytometry compared to NTC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data and TIDE analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cells transduced with sgRNAs targeting Rfx5 failed to induce the surface expression of MHCII following IFNγ stimulation.
source: In cells expressing the non-targeting sgRNA, IFNγ stimulation resulted in a 20-fold increase in MHCII. In contrast, cells transduced with either of two independent sgRNAs targeting Rfx5 failed to induce the surface expression of MHCII following IFNγ stimulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Only IFNγ significantly altered the expression of MHCII among tested stimuli (IFNγ, LPS, Pam3CSK4, IFN-β, TNF and NG-MDP).
source: L3 cells were stimulated with IFNγ, LPS, Pam3CSK4, IFN-β, TNF and N-glycolylated muramyldipeptide (NG-MDP) and 24 hours later the surface expression of MHCII and PD-L1 was quantified. While each stimuli increased PD-L1 expression, only IFNγ significantly altered the expression of MHCII (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D ).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The genome-wide CRISPR screen identified known components of the IFNγ-receptor signal transduction pathway including Ifngr1, Ifngr2, Jak1 and Stat1.
source: As expected, sgRNAs targeting known components of the IFNγ-receptor signal transduction pathway, such as Ifngr1, Ifngr2, Jak1 and Stat1, as well as regulators and components of IFNγ−mediated MHCII expression, such as Ciita, Rfx5, and Rfxank were all significantly enriched (Figure 1D; Reith et al., 2005; Schroder et al., 2004).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the screen results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The genome-wide CRISPR screen identified regulators and components of IFNγ−mediated MHCII expression including Ciita, Rfx5, and Rfxank.
source: As expected, sgRNAs targeting known components of the IFNγ-receptor signal transduction pathway, such as Ifngr1, Ifngr2, Jak1 and Stat1, as well as regulators and components of IFNγ−mediated MHCII expression, such as Ciita, Rfx5, and Rfxank were all significantly enriched (Figure 1D; Reith et al., 2005; Schroder et al., 2004).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the screen results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: For 9 of 15 candidate genes validated from the screen, both gene-specific sgRNAs showed a significant reduction in MHCII surface expression.
source: For all 15 candidates, we observed no changes in basal MHCII expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F) but found deficient MHCII induction following IFNγ stimulation with at least one sgRNA (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2G). For 9 of 15 candidate genes, we observed a significant reduction in MHCII surface expression with both gene-specific sgRNAs
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry validation data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: MED16 was the sixth ranked candidate from the screen results.
source: MED16 was the sixth ranked candidate from our screen results, with robust enrichment of all four sgRNAs in the MHCIIlow population (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the screen ranking data and Figure 2A.

claim: MED16 is uniquely required among the mediator complex subunits for IFNγ-dependent MHCII expression.
source: To examine if MED16 was uniquely required for IFNγ-dependent MHCII expression, we probed our genetic screen data for all mediator complex subunits. The other 27 mediator complex subunits in our library did not show any significant changes in MHCII expression (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by screen data (Figure 2B) and validation experiments (Figure 2C and D).

claim: Med1, Med12 and Med17 targeted cells showed similar MHCII upregulation compared to NTC cells following IFNγ treatment.
source: In support of the screen results, Med1, Med12 and Med17 showed similar MHCII upregulation compared to NTC cells, while Med16 targeted cells demonstrated defects in MHCII surface expression (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Loss of MED16 significantly inhibited the induction of both Ciita and H2aa following IFNγ treatment.
source: Loss of MED16 significantly inhibited the induction of both Ciita and H2aa.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Loss of RFX5 did not impact the induction of Ciita, but had a profound defect in the expression of H2aa compared to NTC cells.
source: Using qRT-PCR, we observed that loss of RFX5 did not impact the induction of Ciita, but had a profound defect in the expression of H2aa compared to NTC cells (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Med16 KO macrophages had significantly reduced MHCII expression when co-cultured with activated NK cells.
source: While co-culture of NTC macrophages with wild type NK cells robustly induced MHCII on the surface, Med16 KO macrophages had significantly reduced MHCII expression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by NK cell co-culture experiments shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Induction of MHCII on macrophages by NK cells was entirely dependent on NK cell-derived IFNγ.
source: In this model, induction of MHCII on macrophages was entirely dependent on NK cell-derived IFNγ as antibody-mediated blockade of IFNγ signaling or co-culture with IFNγ-/- NK cells did not significantly change macrophage surface expression of MHCII.
evidence: This is demonstrated by NK cell co-culture experiments with blocking antibodies and IFNγ-/- NK cells shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Loss of Gsk3b significantly inhibited the expression of both CIITA and H2-Aa after IFNγ-treatment compared to NTC controls.
source: Loss of Gsk3b significantly inhibited the expression of both CIITA and H2-Aa after IFNγ-treatment compared to NTC controls (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Inhibition of GSK3α/β activity with CHIR99021 reduced the induction of surface MHCII and was more deleterious than genetic loss of Gsk3β alone.
source: Inhibition of GSK3α/β activity reduced the induction of surface MHCII and was more deleterious than genetic loss of Gsk3β alone (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data with CHIR99021 treatment shown in Figure 3E.

claim: CHIR99021 treatment of Gsk3b KO macrophages further reduced surface MHCII expression after IFNγ-stimulation compared to the Gsk3b KO alone.
source: To test this hypothesis, we treated Gsk3b KO macrophages with CHIR99021 or DMSO and quantified MHCII surface expression. In support of an important regulatory role for GSK3α, CHIR99021 treatment of Gsk3b KO macrophages further reduced surface MHCII expression after IFNγ-stimulation compared to the Gsk3b KO alone (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Targeting Gsk3a in Gsk3b KO macrophages (double knockout) led to a further reduction of MHCII surface expression, similar to what was observed with CHIR99021 treatment.
source: In contrast, targeting Gsk3a in Gsk3b KO macrophages (i.e. double knockout) led to a further reduction of MHCII surface expression, similar to what was observed with CHIR99021 treatment.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: GSK3α does not compensate for the loss of GSK3β by modulating its expression or activation.
source: To test these hypotheses, NTC and Gsk3b KO cells were left untreated or stimulated with IFNγ for 30 min. We measured total and phosphorylated GSK3α by immunoblot and observed no significant difference between resting and IFNγ activation NTC and Gsk3b KO macrophages (Figure 3H). We observed robust phosphorylation of STAT1 further suggesting this pathway remains intact even in the absence of GSK3β. Together these data suggests that GSK3α does not compensate for the loss of GSK3β by modulating its expression or activation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: GSK3α/β activity is required early after IFNγ stimulation to activate the transcription of MHCII.
source: When MHCII was quantified by flow cytometry we saw a reduction in MHCII expression when CHIR99021 was added 2 or 6 hours after IFNγ (Figure 3I). CHIR99021 addition at later time points resulted in similar MHCII expression compared to DMSO treated cells. When the expression of H2aa mRNA was quantified from a parallel experiment, a significant reduction in mRNA expression was only observed in macrophages that were treated with CHIR99021 2 hours following IFNγ-activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H). Thus, GSK3α/β activity is required early after IFNγ stimulation to activate the transcription of MHCII.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time course experiments with CHIR99021 shown in Figure 3I.

claim: CHIR99021 treated Med16 KO cells showed no change in MHCII expression after IFNγ stimulation.
source: While DMSO-treated Med16 KO cells showed a reproducible two- to threefold increase in MHCII expression after IFNγ stimulation, CHIR99021 treated Med16 KO cells showed no change whatsoever (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: MED16 and GSK3α/β control IFNγ-mediated Ciita induction and MHCII expression through independent mechanisms.
source: These results suggest that MED16 and GSK3α/β control IFNγ-mediated Ciita induction and MHCII expression through independent mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the additive effects of blocking both pathways shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Blocking mTORC1 with Torin2 resulted in a significant reduction in surface MHCII following IFNγ activation.
source: While Torin2 alone had no effect on MHCII expression, blocking mTORC1 resulted in a significant reduction in surface MHCII following IFNγ activation, consistent with our screen analysis (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data with Torin2 treatment shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Blockade of mTORC1 resulted in a significant increase in IFNγ-dependent PD-L1 expression compared to vehicle controls.
source: In contrast to MHCII, blockade of mTORC1 resulted in a significant increase in IFNγ-dependent PD-L1 expression compared to vehicle controls.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: For all genotypes and treatments, the inhibition of mTORC1 resulted in a significant reduction in MHCII expression and a significant increase in PD-L1.
source: Consistent with our findings above, for all genotypes and treatments the inhibition of mTORC1 resulted in a significant reduction in MHCII expression and a significant increase in PD-L1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: mTORC1 functions independently of Med16 and GSK3α/β to control IFNγ-mediated MHCII expression.
source: Taken together these data suggest that while mTORC1 is required for robust IFNγ-mediated MHCII expression, it functions independently of Med16 and GSK3α/β.
evidence: This is inferred from the additive effects of mTORC1 inhibition in knockout cells shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Both Med16 and Gsk3b knockout macrophages had distinct transcriptional signatures in the absence of cytokine stimulation.
source: Both Med16 and Gsk3b knockout macrophages had distinct transcriptional signatures in the absence of cytokine stimulation, which were further differentiated with IFNγ-stimulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by principal component analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: MED16 and GSK3β control distinct transcriptional networks in macrophages following IFNγ-activation.
source: The PCA analysis suggested that MED16 and GSK3β control distinct transcriptional networks in macrophages following IFNγ-activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 5A and differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Neither GSK3β nor MED16 are global regulators of the IFNγ response in macrophages.
source: This suggests that neither GSK3β nor MED16 are global regulators of the IFNγ response in macrophages, but rather are likely to exert their effect on particular genes at the level of transcription or further downstream.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that many IFNγ-regulated genes including Irf1 and GBP genes were unaffected by loss of either gene (Figure 5D).

claim: Eight genes out of the top 20 IFNγ-regulated transcripts were unaffected by loss of either Gsk3b and Med16, including Irf1 and canonical STAT1-target genes (Gbp2, Gbp3, Gbp5, Gbp6 and Gbp7).
source: Hierarchical clustering found that, of the 20 most induced IFNγ-regulated transcripts, the expression of eight were unaffected by loss of either Gsk3b and Med16 (Figure 5D, Cluster 2). Importantly, these genes included a major regulator of the IFNγ response, Irf1, as well as canonical STAT1-target genes (Gbp2, Gbp3, Gbp5, Gbp6 and Gbp7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq data and hierarchical clustering shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Only two genes out of the top 20 IFNγ-regulated genes were similarly reduced in both Med16 KO and Gsk3b KO cells, one of which was H2ab1.
source: In contrast, only two genes, out of the top 20 IFNγ-regulated genes, were similarly reduced in both Med16 KO and Gsk3b KO cells (Cluster 4), one of which was H2ab1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq data and hierarchical clustering shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Stringent differential gene expression analysis of the IFNγ-stimulated transcriptomes identified 69 and 90 significantly different genes for MED16 and GSK3β respectively.
source: Further stringent differential gene expression analysis (FDR < 0.05, absolute LFC > 1) of the IFNγ-stimulated transcriptomes identified 69 and 90 significantly different genes for MED16 and GSK3β respectively.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: Eight non-MHCII genes were shared between MED16 and GSK3β differentially expressed genes, including five genes involved in controlling the extracellular matrix (Mmmp8, Mmp12, Tnn, and Clec12a).
source: Of these differentially expressed genes (DEGs), eight non-MHCII genes were shared between MED16 and GSK3β, including five genes that are involved in controlling the extracellular matrix (Mmmp8, Mmp12, Tnn, and Clec12a).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: Med16 KO cells showed an elevated type I interferon transcriptional response when stimulated with IFNγ.
source: We also observed an elevated type I interferon transcriptional response in Med16 KO cells stimulated with IFNγ that included components of IFNα/β signal transduction (Ifnar2), transcription factors (Stat2, Irf7) and antiviral mediators (Oas2, Ifitm1, Ifitm2, Ifitm3, Ifitm6) (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq data and GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: The effect of Med16 on IFNγ-mediated MHCII expression is cell-autonomous.
source: While Med16 KO cells were unable to robustly induce MHCII, NTC cells from the same well induced MHCII over 30-fold (Figure 5H). These data suggest that the effect of Med16 on IFNγ-mediated MHCII expression is cell-autonomous.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-culture experiments shown in Figure 5H.

claim: DEG analysis of unstimulated macrophages identified 284 differentially expressed genes due to Gsk3b loss.
source: DEG analysis of unstimulated macrophages identified 284 differentially expressed genes due to Gsk3b loss.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: Only macrophages that were treated with IFNγ and pulsed with Cta1 peptide were capable of stimulating NR1 cells to produce IFNγ.
source: Five hours later, we harvested T cells and used intracellular cytokine staining to identify IFNγ producing cells by flow cytometry. Only macrophages that were treated with IFNγ and pulsed with Cta1 peptide were capable of stimulating NR1 cells to produce IFNγ (Figure 6A-C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by T cell activation assay data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Rfx5 deficient macrophages pulsed with peptide in the presence and absence of IFNγ showed limited IFNγ production by NR1 cells in both conditions.
source: Additionally, when Rfx5 deficient macrophages were pulsed with peptide in the presence and absence of IFNγ, we observed limited IFNγ production by NR1 cells in both conditions suggesting this approach is peptide-specific and sensitive to macrophage MHCII surface expression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by T cell activation assay data shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Loss of Gsk3a did not inhibit the production of IFNγ by NR1 cells.
source: In agreement with our findings on MHCII expression, loss of Gsk3a did not inhibit the production of IFNγ by NR1 cells (Figure 6D-F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by T cell activation assay data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: Gsk3b KO cells reduced the number of IFNγ+ NR1 cells over twofold and reduced the mean fluorescence intensity of IFNγ production over 4-fold.
source: In contrast, Gsk3b KO cells reduced the number of IFNγ+ NR1 cells over twofold and reduced the mean fluorescence intensity of IFNγ production over 4-fold.
evidence: This is demonstrated by T cell activation assay data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: Macrophages deficient in Gsk3a and Gsk3b were almost entirely blocked in their ability to activate IFNγ production by NR1 cells.
source: Furthermore, macrophages deficient in Gsk3a and Gsk3b were almost entirely blocked in their ability to activate IFNγ production by NR1 cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by T cell activation assay data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: NR1 cells stimulated on IFNγ-activated Med16 KO macrophages were reduced in the number of IFNγ+ T cells by 10-fold and the fluorescence intensity of IFNγ by 100-fold compared to NTC.
source: NR1 cells stimulated on IFNγ-activated Med16 KO macrophages were reduced in the number of IFNγ+ T cells by 10-fold and the fluorescence intensity of IFNγ by 100-fold compared to NTC (Figure 6G-I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by T cell activation assay data shown in Figure 6G-I.

claim: Treatment of Med16 KO macrophages with CHIR99021 prior to IFNγ-stimulation and T cell co-incubation eliminated the remaining IFNγ production by NR1 cells.
source: Treatment of Med16 KO macrophages with CHIR99021 prior to IFNγ-stimulation and T cell co-incubation, eliminated the remaining IFNγ production by NR1 cells seen in the DMSO treated Med16 KO condition.
evidence: This is demonstrated by T cell activation assay data shown in Figure 6G-I.

claim: GSK3β and MED16 are critical regulators of IFNγ mediated antigen presentation in macrophages and their loss prevents the effective activation of CD4+ T cells.
source: Altogether these results show that GSK3β and MED16 are critical regulators of IFNγ mediated antigen presentation in macrophages and their loss prevents the effective activation of CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the T cell activation assay results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The genome-wide CRISPR screen correctly identified major regulators of IFNγ-signaling.
source: The screen correctly identified major regulators of IFNγ-signaling, highlighting the specificity and robustness of the approach.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the identification of known pathway components like Ifngr1, Jak1, Stat1, etc. in the screen results.

claim: The high rate of validation of screen candidates suggests many new regulatory mechanisms of IFNγ-inducible MHCII expression in macrophages.
source: While we validated only a subset of these candidates, the high rate of validation suggests many new regulatory mechanisms of IFNγ-inducible MHCII expression in macrophages.
evidence: This is inferred from the validation results showing 9 of 15 candidates confirmed with both sgRNAs.

claim: The screen identified an important role for mTOR signaling pathway in controlling IFNγ-mediated MHCII surface expression.
source: While the major pathways identified from the candidates in CRISPR screen were related to IFNγ-signaling, we also identified an important role for other pathways including the mTOR signaling cascade.
evidence: This is based on KEGG pathway analysis of screen hits and experimental validation with Torin2.

claim: Several genes related to metabolism and lysosome function including Lamtor2 and Lamtor4 were found in the top 100 candidates of the screen.
source: Within the top 100 candidates of the screen several genes related to metabolism and lysosome function including Lamtor2 and Lamtor4 were found.
evidence: This is based on the screen results and candidate gene analysis.

claim: MED16 is a subunit of the mediator complex that is critical to recruit RNA polymerase II to the transcriptional start site.
source: MED16 is a subunit of the mediator complex that is critical to recruit RNA polymerase II to the transcriptional start site (Poss et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Individual mediator subunits can control distinct transcriptional networks by interacting with specific transcription factors.
source: While the core mediator complex function is required for many RNA polymerase II dependent transcripts, distinct sub-units of the mediator complex can also play unique roles in gene regulation (Poss et al., 2013; Conaway and Conaway, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MED16 controls NRF2 related signaling networks that respond to oxidative stress.
source: One recent study showed that MED16 controls NRF2 related signaling networks that respond to oxidative stress (Sekine et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: CDK8 controls a subset of IFNγ-dependent gene transcription.
source: Previous studies showed that CDK8, a kinase that can associate with the mediator complex, controls a subset of IFNγ-dependent gene transcription (Bancerek et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: MED16 acts independently of CDK8 in controlling IFNγ-mediated gene expression.
source: However, our results strongly support a model where MED16 acts independently of CDK8. Not only was CDK8 not identified in the initial CRISPR screen, but our transcriptional profiling showed that the major IFNγ-dependent genes controlled by Cdk8, Tap1 and Irf1, remain unchanged in Med16 KO macrophages.
evidence: This is inferred from the screen results and RNA-seq data showing Irf1 is unaffected in Med16 KO cells.

claim: GSK3α and GSK3β are multifunctional kinases that regulate diverse cellular functions including inflammatory and developmental cascades.
source: GSK3α and GSK3β are multifunctional kinases that regulate diverse cellular functions including inflammatory and developmental cascades (Wu and Pan, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: GSK3β and GSK3α coordinate IFNγ-mediated MHCII expression, with GSK3β playing a primary role and GSK3α contributing in the absence of GSK3β.
source: Our studies found that GSK3β and GSK3α coordinate IFNγ-mediated MHCII expression, with GSK3β playing a primary role and GSK3α contributing in the absence of GSK3β.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with Gsk3b KO cells and CHIR99021 treatment or Gsk3a/Gsk3b double knockout.

claim: GSK3 controls IFNγ mediated STAT3 activation, LPS-mediated nitric oxide production, and IRF1 transcriptional activity according to previous studies.
source: Previous studies suggested that GSK3 controls IFNγ mediated STAT3 activation, LPS-mediated nitric oxide production, and IRF1 transcriptional activity but our transcriptional results clearly show these do not explain the requirement for GSK3-dependent MHCII expression (Beurel and Jope, 2008; Huang et al., 2009; Garvin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature, but the authors' data contradicts this for MHCII regulation.

claim: IFNγ primed macrophages activate mTORC1 resulting in blunted TLR2 responses in human monocyte-derived macrophages.
source: Work in human monocyte-derived macrophages showed previously that IFNγ primed macrophages activate mTORC1 resulting in blunted TLR2 responses opposite of the results from the MHCII genetic screen (Su et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: mTORC1 differentially controls the expression of distinct IFNγ-inducible genes.
source: Our study provides new evidence that mTORC1 differentially controls the expression of distinct IFNγ-inducible genes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing opposite effects of mTORC1 inhibition on MHCII (reduced) versus PD-L1 (increased).

claim: mTOR activity was required for robust IFNγ-mediated MHCII expression.
source: In contrast, mTOR activity was required for robust IFNγ-mediated MHCII expression, in agreement with the bioinformatic analysis from our screen.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with Torin2 showing reduced MHCII expression.

claim: mTORC1 inhibition further diminished MHCII expression in Gsk3b KO or CHIR99021 cells suggesting GSK3α/β functions independently of mTOR to control IFNγ-inducible MHCII.
source: We also observed that mTORC1 inhibition further diminished MHCII expression in Gsk3b KO or CHIR99021 cells suggesting GSK3α/β functions independently of mTOR to control IFNγ-inducible MHCII.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments combining mTORC1 inhibition with GSK3 loss/inhibition shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Inhibition or loss of GSK3 results in the constitutive stabilization of Beta-Catenin and Tcf expression.
source: Inhibition or loss of GSK3 results in the constitutive stabilization of Beta-Catenin and Tcf expression.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about GSK3 function in Wnt signaling.

claim: Fzd4, a Wnt signaling pathway member, was identified in the screen as required for MHCII expression.
source: Interestingly, another Wnt signaling pathway member Fzd4 was identified in our screen as required for MHCII expression in our screen, supporting a possible role for Wnt in IFNγ-induced MHCII regulation.
evidence: This is based on the screen results.

claim: GSK3 was recently found to be co-opted by the Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium effector SteE to skew infected macrophage polarization.
source: GSK3 was recently found to be co-opted by the Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium effector SteE to skew infected macrophage polarization and allow infection to persist (Gibbs et al., 2020; Panagi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Salmonella and other pathogens including M. tuberculosis and C. trachomatis modulate the expression of MHCII.
source: While it is known that Salmonella and other pathogens including M. tuberculosis and C. trachomatis, modulate the expression of MHCII, the precise mechanisms underlying many of these virulence tactics remains unclear (Alix et al., 2020; Ankley et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Conditional knockout mice were recently developed for GSK3α and Gsk3β.
source: Conditional knockout mice were recently developed for GSK3α and Gsk3β and can now be used to specifically ablate Gsk3b in macrophages in vivo and examine IFNγ responses.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about available research tools.
